opus-5.5.text:
I think the most immediate change is just how much time people get back. If you add up cooking, cleaning, laundry, tidying, and general maintenance, a typical household spends a few hours a day on this stuff. If a robot can reliably do most of that, it's not a marginal convenience. It's comparable to the shift we saw when washing machines and dishwashers came in, except it covers a much wider range of tasks.

That changes how people relate to their space. Right now a lot of decisions about a home are constrained by upkeep. People avoid bigger houses, gardens, certain materials, or having lots of things around because it's all work to maintain. If maintenance becomes nearly free, those tradeoffs shift. You might see people choosing larger or more elaborate living spaces, or keeping things that are a hassle today, like fresh home-cooked meals every day, without that being a burden on anyone in the family.

There's also a distributional angle that's easy to overlook. Historically, only fairly wealthy households could afford domestic staff. A capable household robot is essentially making that kind of service available to a much broader population, once costs come down. So the experience of having a home that's always clean, where meals are prepared and errands are handled, could go from being a luxury to something fairly ordinary.

Then there are less obvious effects. Elder care is a big one. A lot of people move out of their homes into assisted living because they can't manage daily tasks on their own. Robots that can help with mobility, cooking, and monitoring could let people stay in their homes much longer. Similarly, parents of young children might find the home becomes much more manageable.

That said, I'd be cautious about timelines. Physical manipulation in messy, unstructured environments like homes is genuinely hard, and robotics has lagged behind progress in language and reasoning models. So I expect the effects to come gradually: first narrower tasks, then more general capability as hardware improves and costs fall. But once robots are general enough to handle the long tail of household tasks, I think the change is going to be quite profound, probably more than people intuitively expect.

r001.rationale: The response says reduced upkeep could lead people to choose larger or more elaborate homes. It does not suggest needing less living space by rearranging the same space for different activities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that people tend to underestimate how much of what happens in a home is just maintenance. If you actually tally up the hours, a lot of what people do at home is cleaning, cooking, laundry, tidying, moving things around, dealing with small repairs. That's a huge fraction of non-work time, and it's mostly not time people enjoy. So the most immediate effect of capable household robots is that a lot of that just disappears from people's lives, the same way that washing machines and dishwashers already removed a big chunk of it in the 20th century. But this time it's much more general, because the robot isn't a single-purpose appliance, it can do whatever a person would have done.

Once that happens, I think the way people use the space itself starts to change. Right now homes are designed around the assumption that humans do the upkeep. The kitchen is laid out so a person can reach things, storage is arranged for human convenience, and there's a lot of implicit tolerance for mess because cleaning is costly. If upkeep is essentially free, you can afford to have more things, more complicated setups, more elaborate meals, bigger gardens, and so on, because the cost of maintaining them has collapsed. People might also spend more time at home, because the home becomes a nicer place to be and some of the things you'd currently go out for, like eating at a restaurant, become easier to replicate.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking about this purely in terms of chores, though. The bigger shift is probably that the home becomes a place where a lot of services get delivered that currently require leaving or hiring someone. Elder care is the obvious one. A huge amount of what determines whether an older person can stay in their own home is whether someone can help them with physical tasks, and if a robot can do that, then a lot of people who'd otherwise move into assisted living just don't. Similarly for childcare, for people with disabilities, and so on. So I'd expect the home to absorb functions that are currently outsourced to institutions.

I'd also say the timeline here is more uncertain than for a lot of the software stuff. The hardware is harder, the cost has to come down a lot, and reliability in an unstructured environment like a home is genuinely difficult. So I think we'll see this, but I wouldn't bet it arrives at the same pace as, say, AI doing white-collar work. It's probably one of the later things to be transformed rather than one of the first.

r001.rationale: The response says people may want more things and more elaborate setups as upkeep gets cheaper, but it does not suggest robots could reduce the space people need by rearranging the same space for different activities.

astra-6.text:
I think one interesting possibility is that people could use the same space for more things. Today, you tend to arrange a room for a particular purpose, and changing that arrangement takes effort. If you had a robot that could reliably move furniture around and put things away, you could have a space that serves as an office during the day and then becomes a dining room in the evening.

And more generally, there's a lot of work involved in using your home that makes you less inclined to do things. You might enjoy cooking but dislike cleaning up afterward, or want to have friends over but not want to deal with the mess. If robots could handle that work, it could change what you actually choose to do at home, beyond just saving you some time.

r001.rationale: The response says one space could serve as an office and dining room at different times, but it does not communicate that this could reduce how much living space people need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one interesting possibility is that homes become much more flexible. Today, we tend to give each room a fairly fixed purpose, partly because rearranging furniture and moving things around is a hassle. If you had a robot that could do that reliably, you could use a space as an office during the day, turn it into a dining room in the evening, and perhaps a bedroom at night.

And then, of course, there’s the more straightforward benefit of having someone—or something—do the dishes, the laundry, and the cleaning. That could change how much time people spend maintaining their homes, but also how they use them. You might be more willing to cook or have friends over if you didn’t have to think about all the work afterward. So I’d expect both a reduction in household labor and some changes in what people actually want their homes to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes using the same room for different activities at different times, but does not suggest this could reduce how much living space people need.
